item.title: Knee — Positional Release / Counterstrain
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Knee and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: knee flexion/extension, patellofemoral/tibiofemoral symptoms and functional loading.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, prone or sitting with the knee supported in the position required by the technique.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the knee with hands close to the joint line and the limb fully supported.
stabilization: Stabilize femur, tibia or patella depending on the target.
contact: Use broad contact and avoid sustained compression over the fibular head/common peroneal nerve.
Locate a reproducible tender point with light palpation, then monitor it while positioning the region toward maximal comfort.
Do not maintain painful pressure on the tender point.
forceDirection: The treatment direction is indirect: shorten/unload the painful tissue until tenderness is substantially reduced, then hold without force.
dosage: Traditional teaching often uses about 90 seconds, individualized to comfort and response.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Knee: knee flexion/extension, patellofemoral/tibiofemoral symptoms and functional loading.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Avoid routine manual therapy with suspected DVT, fracture, acute instability, infection or uncleared postoperative restriction.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Knee assessment → correct regional setup → Positional Release / Counterstrain → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Hamstring Tender Point — Positional Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce focal posterior-thigh/knee tenderness and guarding before active loading.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine or prone. Flex the knee and adjust hip position until the tender point becomes substantially less sensitive.
subTechniques.contact: Light monitoring contact over the symptomatic hamstring area; support the limb fully.
subTechniques.direction: Maintain the shortened position with no stretch force.
subTechniques.dosage: 60–90 seconds, then slowly lengthen the limb back to neutral.
subTechniques.reassess: Tenderness, knee extension tolerance and active knee flexion.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: This is a comfort-based technique; it should not feel like a hamstring stretch.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid acute muscle tear or significant bruising.

subTechniques.name: Popliteus Region — Positional Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce selected posterolateral knee guarding after serious pathology has been excluded.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the knee comfortably flexed. Fine-tune small tibial rotation and knee-flexion position until the tender region becomes easier.
subTechniques.contact: Use a gentle posterolateral monitoring contact and avoid deep pressure into the popliteal fossa.
subTechniques.direction: Hold the position of ease without compressing posterior neurovascular structures.
subTechniques.dosage: About 60 seconds with close symptom monitoring.
subTechniques.reassess: Posterolateral tenderness, knee extension/flexion and gait.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: The popliteal fossa contains vulnerable structures—contact should stay broad and superficial.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Do not use with suspected DVT, acute vascular symptoms or unexplained calf swelling.
